## Act 114 — A switched-off app blamed the server

Opening Broadcasts on a business whose Email module was off gave:

> **Could not load your broadcasts** · Something went wrong reaching the server.
> Try again in a moment. **[ Try again ]**

Nothing had gone wrong. The account had Email switched off, api-rest answered its
module gate with a 404 exactly as designed, and the console turned that into an
accusation against the server plus a button that could not work on the first
press or the hundredth.

### The fourth state

A pane's content had three shapes and each had a home — waiting, empty, could not
load. A surface belonging to an inactive module is none of them, so it fell into
the third. `PaneLoadError` could not have rescued it either: `MODULE_DISABLED`
IS a 404, so a pane that passed its error along would have said "that broadcast
is no longer here", which is a different lie.

Fixed at the MOUNT rather than in the panes. There are 215 surfaces in one
console and 99 in the other, and **166 of them never passed their error to
`PaneLoadError` at all** — so asking per-pane is 166 chances to have already
forgotten. `SurfaceBody` asks once, using `surfaceIsVisible`, the predicate the
rail and the command palette already share. Its own comment asks for exactly
that: the rail and the launcher disagreeing about what exists is the bug it was
written to prevent.

### A gate that existed and failed open

`deep-link-resolve.ts` already had this gate, and it let me straight through —
which is how the pane opened at all. It answered `ok` while the module list was
loading, and on a cold arrival it always is. The file's own doc claimed the
opposite. It waits now.

### The two brands do not say the same thing

sparx sells modules one at a time, so the way back is a button to Settings →
Modules. **Piggles is one plan with everything in it** — its own All apps dialog
says "every one of them is included and working" — and it hides the module
pricing screen on purpose. Measured: 0 of 8 Piggles businesses have a module off.
So under Piggles this is not a setting anybody chose but an account missing
something it is entitled to, and it says that instead of offering a switch that
does not exist.

**My first draft got that wrong** and shipped one button for both consoles,
pointing at a surface Piggles does not have. Clicking it opened `link-not-found`.
Only looking caught it.

[457].

## Act 115 — Social, opened for the first time, and a pane that named itself

Devi has never used Social: zero connections, zero posts, zero of everything the
eight panes hold. So this act is the **first-run experience of a whole app**,
which is what every new Piggles business meets and what nobody had looked at.

She found it through **All apps → Get Found**, which describes itself as "Help
people find you in search and on social" — the right door, and Piggles' own words
throughout: **What is going out, and when · Posts · How your posts did · Comments
and replies · Posts waiting on you · How often you post · Your social accounts**.

### The first-run flow half held

Clicking a day opens the composer beside the calendar, and that part does the
right thing:

> **Connect an account to start posting**
> There is nowhere for a post to go yet. Connect a page or profile — your Facebook
> Page, Instagram, Google Business listing — and it shows up here as a destination
> you can write to.

That is a proper gate: it will not let her write into a void, and its button lands
on Connections. Facebook, Instagram and Threads connect; six more say **Coming
soon** and say why. A beta banner is honest about the networks still reviewing
access, and promises nothing she writes is lost.

**The three screens before it did not know that.** The calendar said "click any
day to write your first one"; Posts offered only **New post**; and How your posts
did said "open a post you have already sent" — an instruction naming a thing she
has never had. All three end at the composer explaining she cannot, and sending
her back.

None of it needed a request. `useSocialBoard` **already returns the overview** to
both the calendar and Posts, and Insights was already calling it twice for the
account avatars. Three panes holding the answer, none drawing it
([[feedback_fetched_but_never_rendered]]). One derived flag in the shared hook,
three sentences, and Posts' primary button is now **Connect an account** — the
same decision the composer already made, one screen earlier so the detour never
happens. [459].

**Not driven end to end.** Connecting an account is a real OAuth sign-in to a live
social network, so the composer, the queue, approvals, insights and the inbox have
all been seen EMPTY and none has been seen with a post in it. That is a real gap
in this act, not a completed pass.

### The defect: a pane that named itself, in the wrong language

Four of those tabs did not say what the rail said. They said **Inbox**,
**Approvals**, **Cadence**, **Connections** — and three sat in one strip next to
**How your posts did**, which was right, so both behaviours were on screen at once.

A tab has two possible authors: the catalog title, which goes through
`vocabulary.ts`, and `ctx.setTitle`, which does not — it is the OPERATOR's rename
slot and therefore outranks the registry, because `INV-000004` has to beat
`Invoice`. A surface handing back its own name pins the tab to the platform's word.

Measured: **52 surfaces did it** across both consoles. Eight already showed a name
used nowhere else; the other 44 restated one nobody had changed yet, which is not a
lie but a lie in waiting. Worst of the eight: a settings tab reading **"How the CRM
behaves"** — a technical acronym `check:piggles-nav` explicitly bans, on a product
whose promise is that she never meets one.

The rule now lives at the chokepoint (`isOwnStaticTitle`): an own-name is cleared
rather than stored, so the pane keeps answering to the registry. The 54 dead
effects were swept; the script refused on the two files that were not the exact
shape, and **both refusals turned out to be further defects** — sparx titled every
page check "Page check" (three open checks, three identical tabs) and its cart pane
was titled from two places at once.

### It was written down in three places, and I found the third by clicking

The wrong word was **saved**, not just rendered, and each copy hid the next.

1. Our descriptors. Swept on load — nothing else would remove them now the effects
   are gone.
2. **dockview's own grid blob**, which our persistence comment calls "opaque to us
   by design — it owns layout". It owns layout AND kept a private copy of every tab
   label, and on restore that copy wins.
3. **The windows-mode snapshot.** I reasoned this one was safe. Then I clicked the
   toggle and the tab said **Connections** again.

The check that exists for exactly this class, `check:piggles-nav`, passed
throughout. It labels a surface `pane tab` in its own output, so it believed it
covered this; it was reading the name the tab was SUPPOSED to have. Now scans
`ctx.setTitle` too — 28 previously unchecked strings, and reinstating one line
reddens it by name.

[458].

## Act 116 — Money, opened for the first time

Ten Money panes, never opened. Devi has real money moving through them: 16 orders,
8 payments, 3 refunds, 10 invoices, $1,645.50 outstanding — and, at the start,
zero costs and twenty platform-seeded spending categories.

The panel reads beautifully. Three sections framed as questions an owner asks —
**Money coming in · Money going out · Did you make money** — and inside them
**Money paid to you · Owed to you · Where money comes from · Spending · Bills to
pay · Repeating costs · Who you pay · What you kept · By job**.

Four defects, every one found by asking the database what the answer should be
BEFORE looking at the screen, then comparing.

### The money that went back was not on the screen

Payments showed Anneliese Vogt's $170.00 with **−$128.00 back**. $170.00 had gone
back. Jo Kim's $147.00 showed nothing back; $42.00 had.

The refund total grouped on `paymentId`, which is NULLABLE — and a refund raised
by the RETURNS flow has none, because it is against the ORDER. Platform-wide,
**10 of 12 refunds have no payment: $7,767 of $8,316.** The screen was showing 7%
of the money that had gone back. The order's own `refundTotal` was right all
along, because the rollup that maintains it reads by order at a documented
chokepoint. [460].

### Two bills due the same day, one late and one not

Eight invoices printed **Due Sep 8**. Seven said "1 day late", one said "Not yet
due" — and $234.60 sat in the wrong aging bucket. Lateness was elapsed
milliseconds; INV-000001 was raised at noon, so only 0.93 of a 24-hour period had
passed. The date she READS is formatted as a UTC calendar day on purpose.

**Five separate copies** of "how late is this bill" — the aging report, this
screen, the dunning ladder's exact-day predicate, the B2B credit-hold ladder, and
a raw SQL scan. One shared `daysPastDue` now. The existing tests all used midnight
due dates, where both rules agree, so the wrong one passed them perfectly. [461].

### She recorded a cost and was told she had recorded nothing

$240.00 of fabric. Toast: "Cost recorded". Status bar: "Saved just now". The list
below: **"$0.00 · 0 costs · Nothing recorded yet"**, and Refresh changed nothing.

The range `?to=2026-09-09` was filtered `lte` midnight, so a range ending TODAY
contained none of today. Everything she entered would have been invisible until
tomorrow — and the obvious next move is to type it again. The accounting export
carried the same bound, so the last day of every period sent to her accountant was
short. The period picker's own comment states the contract the server broke:
"Ranges are calendar-boundary DATES, not instants." [462].

### "Updated just now", over figures from breakfast

"What you kept" is a cache rebuilt once a day (revenue 06:00 UTC, profit 06:45),
and its refresh marker showed when the BROWSER last fetched. A page opened at 5pm
said "updated just now" over numbers from breakfast. The rollup has recorded
`computed_at` on every rebuild since it shipped, read by nobody. [463].

**One question left for Brandon**, because it costs money: closing the underlying
staleness needs either a reconcile on the read path or a new consumer keeping the
revenue rollup fresh. The marker makes the screen honest; making it live is a
spend decision.

### What did NOT turn out to be a defect

Two things chased and dropped, both worth recording because the reasoning is the
work. The order numbers render in a face where `O` and `0` look alike — read out
of the DOM the character is a real capital O, and no order number starts with a
digit, so there is nothing to confuse it with. And `finance/channels.ts` looked
like the same date bug as [462] until I checked what its client sends: an instant,
not a calendar date, so its `lte` is correct. I had already changed it, and
reverted.

[460] · [461] · [462] · [463].

## Act 117 — The last six Money panes, and a query nobody could see was wrong

Six panes left. Same method as act 116: work out what each screen should say from
the database first, then open it.

**Money paid to you** was empty, and right to be. Devi's eight payments are cash,
checks and a gift card; the screen only shows deposits that ARRIVE from a card
processor, and its empty state says exactly that without being asked — _"Cash,
checks and account payments don't appear here: they're money you've received, not
a deposit that arrives."_ That is the best-written empty state in the module.

**Where money comes from** agreed with the database to the cent. Two cancelled
orders worth $252.60 are correctly excluded, which is why the screen's 11
website orders and $2,140.50 look short against the raw 13 and $2,393.10.

**Repeating costs** and **Who you pay** are both empty and both say something
useful about what would fill them. "Catch up now" is correctly disabled with
nothing to catch up.

Then the last four defects.

### She was told she owed $2,090 to nobody

**Bills to pay** opened on **"Total outstanding $2,090.00 across 2 bills"**.

Those two bills are the rent and the linen she recorded in act 116. Both were
paid before she typed them in. Nothing she entered said otherwise.

The Spending quick-add is three fields and a button, deliberately, and writes
`paidAt: null, dueAt: null` — the honest record of what she said, which is that a
cost happened. This screen read the absence of a payment date as a debt.

The file's own header knew about the receipt someone types in, and stopped one
clause short: it guarded the LATENESS ("not late, it is simply unpaid") and then
summed the same row into the total anyway. Not late, and not owed either, was the
half that was missing. The aging bar made it louder rather than quieter, drawing
a full-width "No due date" band worth the whole figure.

The headline now counts what has a day to pay it by. The rest is listed, and
said, and left out: _"Not counted above: $2,090.00 across 2 costs with no due
date. Recording a cost does not say whether you have paid it."_

The smaller fix — stamp `paidAt` in the quick-add, since a receipt is proof of
payment — I considered and rejected. Writing "paid today" when she never said so
invents a fact in the other direction. The screen should claim neither, and now
does. Issue [465](issues/465-she-was-told-she-owed-2090-dollars-to-nobody.md).

### By job never worked, for anybody, and typecheck could not tell

**By job** sat on "Just a moment…". Every request it makes in its DEFAULT filter
answered **500**:

```
types=order    → 200
types=booking  → 500
(no types)     → 500   ← the default
```

The query asked a booking for its `customer`. `Booking` has no such relation,
deliberately, and its schema says so two fields away: scheduling stays unaware
that CRM exists, so a booking carries a bare `customerId` and nothing to join.

**TypeScript cannot see this.** Measured, on a file that typechecks clean:
`where: { notAColumn: true }` is TS2353, and `select: { customer: {…} }` compiles.
A generated `<Model>Select` is a mapped type over a type parameter, and
excess-property checking never runs on one. I confirmed tsc covers the file
before believing it, by breaking something else in the same function.

So I asked the whole repo. A new `pnpm check:prisma-selects` reads the field list
from the schema and validates every select key with the TypeScript parser:
**6,213 fields across 422 models, six wrong, four files.** Two of the others are
worse than this one — the ticket resolver threw before reading a single field, so
every automation keyed on a ticket has been dead, and both halves of the offer
stack threw whenever an offer was picked. Wired into the pre-push guard and CI.
Issue [464](issues/464-a-screen-that-answered-500-because-a-query-named-a-field-that-does-not-exist.md).

### And then it blamed her internet

Waiting out that failure produced the next one. After twenty-five seconds of
retries the pane said **"The server could not be reached."**

It was reached. It answered in 57 milliseconds, and its answer was that it had
failed. A shop owner reading that goes and looks at her router.

Issue 286 already split "this record is gone" out of "could not be reached". A
5xx is the third cause and was still wearing the first one's sentence. Three
states now, and the new sentence is owned by the component rather than the call
site — every caller's own description is written about the unreachable case, so
one edit reaches all hundred of them and none had to change.
Issue [467](issues/467-a-500-that-told-her-to-check-her-internet.md).

### Thirty sentences still speaking the other product's language

The payouts pane is renamed — the tab reads "Money paid to you" because "payouts"
is the accountant's word. The screen inside it said **"No payouts yet"**.

`check:piggles-nav` exists to stop exactly this and was green. Its four seams all
read a string that passes through SOMETHING: a catalog entry, a copy key, a title
slot. A sentence typed straight into JSX passes through nothing.

Thirty were live. The command palette she opens all day said "Type to search
across every **module**"; Add a site, which she has used seven times, said
"needs the Builder **module**"; filing a product spent fourteen sentences
teaching her the word **collection**, which piggles/CLAUDE.md RULE #3 names
outright as one a person must never be made to learn.

The sharpest one is on the surface seam 4 was built for. Act 115 removed
`setTitle('How the CRM behaves')` from the customer-settings pane; the leave-guard
**five lines below it** went on asking whether to discard "your changes to how the
CRM behaves". Same file, same word, left behind by the fix for the first one.

A fifth seam reads JSX text, text props, and whole sentences in string literals —
that last because the palette's placeholder lives in a ternary. **624 rendered
strings before, 12,335 now.** Two kinds of exemption, both self-destructing: the
two blocks Piggles genuinely does not render (keyed on the feature, and the check
throws if either stops being hidden), and three terms a person must meet because
somebody else's screen says them. Issue
[466](issues/466-thirty-sentences-speaking-the-other-products-language.md).

### Measured and deliberately not filed

While the failing request retried, the pane showed the PREVIOUS filter's rows —
"Appointments" listing two orders under a highlighted Appointments chip. Measured
with the real library: during a failing fetch react-query reports `status:
'success'` with `isPlaceholderData: true` and the old data, and **none of the 155
call sites using that pattern reads the flag.**

I did not file 155 defects. Keeping the last answer while the next loads is
deliberate and normally invisible, and the refresh control already reads as busy
throughout. What made it harmful was a request that could never succeed, and that
is fixed. The measurement is recorded in 467 because it names the mechanism if a
second screen is ever seen doing it.

## Act 118 — Money finished, and three warnings nobody had ever seen

Four Money rows were still unscored after act 117. Three are reachable —
**Spending categories**, **Accounting**, and a **cost's own screen** — and
`finance.payout.detail` is not, because she has no bank deposits to open one on.

Same method: work out the answer from the database first, then look.

**Spending categories** matched: 3 cost-of-the-work, 3 wages, 14 running costs.
The screen is good. It groups by kind rather than listing twenty rows, explains
each group in a sentence, and closes with the reason any of it matters — _"Filing
a cost in the wrong group does not change your bottom line, but it does change
whether a job looks worth doing."_ Changing a category's kind raises a live
warning that past profit figures will move. Archiving one names what is kept.
Delete appears only on an invented category with nothing filed under it, and
never on a built-in one.

**A cost's own screen** is the best-composed detail pane in Money. It carries the
January-bill-paid-in-March distinction in two sentences, splits the cost across
jobs with the remainder named as the cost of being open, and its delete says what
it costs: _"Your profit for that period will change. This cannot be undone."_
Nothing wrong with it.

Then five defects, and the second is the largest thing this persona has turned
up.

### Two categories, one name

Devi added **Packaging & gift wrap**, which her boutique needs and the seeded set
has no word for. Then she added it again, and the server said **201 Created**.

The second copy landed in **Running costs**, because the kind dropdown resets to
its default and she had not touched it. So the same name now sat on both sides of
the gross-profit line, and the picker where a cost is filed showed two identical
lines with nothing to choose between them.

The table has a unique index and it is on `(tenant_id, slug)`. An invented
category has **no slug** — correctly, and `createCategory` says why: the slug
namespace belongs to the seeded set derivers address, and a tenant minting
`wages` would collide with it. Postgres treats NULLs as distinct, so that index
says nothing at all about invented rows, and the NAME was guarded by nothing.

This module guards everything else, each with a typed error and a sentence an
owner can act on. Uniqueness is the one nobody wrote, and the index sitting right
beside it looks like it covers this.

One guard now serves both writers, inside the transaction so it cannot race, case
and space insensitive, and it checks archived rows too — which gives the error two
forms, because "you already have one" about a row that is not on her screen sends
her hunting for something she cannot see. Issue
[468](issues/468-two-categories-one-name.md).

### Every warning a download carried had never once been shown

The Accounting export's default period is **Last month**. Devi opened it on the
9th, so the range was August, and she has no costs in August. She would have
downloaded a file with nothing in it under a toast reading _"Every cost in that
period is in the file."_

I fixed that, reloaded, and the screen said the same thing. Which is how the real
one turned up.

A cross-origin `fetch` can read seven response headers and no others unless the
server names them in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. api-rest set none.
Measured, on the console's own origin:

```js
[...response.headers.keys()]; // → ["content-length", "content-type"]
```

No error, no warning, no failed request. `headers.get(…)` answers null and every
fallback beside it reads as good news:

| tried to read              | got  | what the person saw                         |
| -------------------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `content-disposition`      | null | every export saved as `expenses.csv`        |
| `content-disposition`      | null | every timesheet saved as `hours.csv`        |
| `x-sparx-skipped-rows`     | `0`  | "Every cost in that period is in the file." |
| `x-sparx-unpriced-minutes` | `0`  | nothing at all                              |

The last one is the bad one. The timesheet export carries this sentence:

> _"12h 30m are in the hours column but not the cost column — nobody has a pay
> rate covering them. They still have to be paid."_

It has never appeared. Not once, for anybody. Somebody pays staff from that file.

Both routes carry a careful comment about why the fact rides on a header — _"a
download cannot carry a warning"_ — and both authors were defeated by one missing
line of configuration four hundred files away.

`pnpm check:exposed-headers` now reads the allowlist and scans both consoles'
client code for `headers.get('…')`, and also asserts the CORS registration
actually receives the list. Its first version had the bug it exists to catch: an
apostrophe in the prose above an entry paired with the next one and swallowed a
real header. It strips comments now, and refuses anything that does not parse as
a header name. Issue
[469](issues/469-every-warning-a-download-carried-had-never-been-shown.md).

### Said over an empty file, and named after the wrong product

With the headers readable, the two smaller things underneath became fixable.

The empty export now says so, and better, says so **before** she downloads it.
The date range carries a count — _"Aug 1, 2026 to Aug 31, 2026 · no costs
recorded"_, _"Sep 1, 2026 to Sep 9, 2026 · 2 costs"_ — which was free, because the
expenses endpoint already runs an aggregate for its total. Preventing beats
reporting. The toast has three outcomes rather than two, and a missing row-count
header reads as **-1, not 0**, because a server that said nothing has not said
zero. Issue
[470](issues/470-every-cost-is-in-the-file-said-over-an-empty-file.md).

And the file itself downloaded as
**`sparx-expenses-csv-2026-08-01-to-2026-08-31.csv`**. Devi has never heard of
sparx. This is the one artifact in the product that LEAVES it — she emails it to
her bookkeeper — so a third party now holds a document naming a product their
client is not paying for. `check:piggles-nav` was green because it scans screens,
and a Downloads folder is not a screen. The timesheet export next door already
had it right: `hours-…`. Issue
[472](issues/472-the-file-she-sends-her-accountant-was-named-after-another-product.md).

### Six rows pointing the wrong way

The "Sending it automatically" card's own heading says _"the export above"_. The
six rows inside it all said **below**, and there is nothing below — that list is
the last thing on the screen.

The sentences live in the finance package and the console decides where the
export card goes, so "below" was a guess. "Above" would be a luckier guess, wrong
again the day either console reorders. The direction word is gone: "the
spreadsheet export **on this screen**" is true wherever it is placed, and all
three sites carry a comment saying why there is none. Issue
[471](issues/471-six-rows-pointed-below-at-something-above-them.md).

### One thing I nearly filed and should not have

I clicked the "Include archived" switch twice, it did not move, and I began
writing it up as a dead control. It works. The first click landed while a confirm
dialog was still closing and the second hit a 1x1 hidden input rather than the
visible track. Clicking the track turned it on, then off again.

The screen was fine and my aim was not.

## Act 119 — Stock, opened for the first time, and four screens that answered without knowing

Money is finished, so the next module. **Stock** is the biggest unopened surface
in the console — 56 panes never looked at against 8 scored — and for a boutique
it is the daily job rather than a monthly one.

Same method as act 118: work out the answer from the database first, then look.
72 stock lines across two locations, 230 versions of 50 garments, 16 days of
trading history, first movement 24 August.

Devi's five panes this act are the planning ones, because they are the ones that
tell her what to buy: **At risk**, **What matters most**, **Not selling**, **Cost
to keep**, and **What to reorder**.

### "$0.00 at risk", before anything had been measured

At risk opened with three figures across the top. The first was **$0.00** in
danger red. She pressed **Work it out now**, which is the only thing the screen
asks of her, and it became **$558.00** — two garments, seven days of cover each,
a fortnight to replace them.

The pane is not careless about this anywhere else. It says "Nothing has been
measured yet" in a banner, "72 stock lines have never been measured" in a second
one, and its empty state is as plain as it gets: _"This list is empty because no
pass has been made over your sales and deliveries — not because everything is
fine."_ Its own header comment states the rule in capitals. The rows follow it.
The empty state follows it. The three biggest numbers on the screen did not, and
a number outranks a paragraph underneath it every time.

`useHasBeenMeasured()` was already imported and already in a variable two lines
above the figures that ignored it — the shape that keeps recurring here, where
the value is in the component's hand and nothing draws it
([473](issues/473-at-risk-said-zero-dollars-over-something-nobody-had-measured.md)).
**Not selling** carried the identical shape in all three of its headline sums and
got the identical fix. Both now say "Not yet", with the reason.

Everything else on At risk checks out to the cent. Forecast 0.4286 a day, three
left, seven days of cover, fourteen days assumed lead time, about three orders
short, $128 x 3 = $384.00. It also says the lead time is **assumed**, which is
the half most screens leave out.

### She was told to write off a fortnight of stock

**Not selling** said 54 of her 72 lines are not selling at all, $870 tied up,
$217.50 a year to keep, and against each one:

> Nothing has ever sold from this. Discount it, bundle it, return it to the
> supplier, or write it off — it is not going to move on its own.

Her stock arrived on 24 August. This was 9 September.

Her dead-stock window is 180 days, which is the default and the number her own
planning settings show her. It was applied to every line that HAD sold and to
none of the lines that had not: a null last sale went straight through as dead.
So the window was 180 days for a shirt that sold in March and **nought days** for
the shirt beside it that arrived on Tuesday
([474](issues/474-stock-was-dead-the-day-it-arrived.md)).

Never having sold is the absence of a sale. It only becomes a finding when a
length of time is attached to it, and none was. A line that has never sold is now
measured from when it arrived, which is one window applied the same way to every
line, and the sentence carries the number of days.

The second half of that is worse and nobody could have seen it. Before any pass
has run there are no velocity rows at all, so **every** line has a null velocity
and a null last sale, so **every** line was dead. A brand-new shop's first look
at this screen listed its entire catalogue as dead stock to write off — and the
pane's carefully written "nothing has been checked yet" empty state was
unreachable, guarded by the very bug it was written for.

Her list is now empty and says the honest thing: _"Everything is moving. Either
the buying is well judged, or there is not enough history yet to tell."_

### Every line was long tail, on a ranking that had nothing to rank

**What matters most** answers "where is the money in my stock". Counted in the
live DOM rather than read:

```
rows: 72 · Worth: { "Long tail": 72 } · Value a year: $0.00 x 72 · Share: 0.00% x 72
```

And the banner above them told her to trust exactly the half that was empty:
_"The left-hand column **is real** — it ranks your stock by what you actually use
in a year, and that only needs totals."_

It needs more than totals. Worth is units used multiplied by what a unit cost,
and an unrecorded cost has to enter that multiplication as a zero for the
arithmetic to run at all. **Three of her 72 stock lines have a cost price, and of
the 17 that have actually sold something, none do.** The entire ranking was
computed on absent data and presented as a finding
([475](issues/475-every-line-was-long-tail-because-nothing-had-a-cost.md)).

The other half of the same pane gets this right, and says so in the schema:
`xyzClass` is nullable on purpose, because it used to default to Z and _"a
catalogue nobody had sold from yet reported every line as erratic"_. That
paragraph sits four lines below `abcClass String @default("C")`.

Now: `No cost price` where the rank was, `No cost set` where the money was, a
count above the table, and a banner that no longer overclaims. LEATHER-BELT —
one of the three that HAS a cost, and genuinely used none of it — still reads
`Long tail / $0.00 / 0.00%`, which is a real zero and a real finding. The two are
finally distinguishable.

### Two screens under one heading, with nothing in common

At risk had just named the two garments worth $558. **What to reorder** listed
one line, and it was neither of them: an out-of-stock shirt that nothing has sold
of in 90 days.

It watches `reorder_point`, the level a person set — which is the right rule, and
the tests say why: _"LEAVES the human number alone — this is the whole consent
rule."_ A system that starts buying off its own arithmetic is worse than one that
waits to be asked. **One of her 72 stock lines has one.**

The screen already handles the case where nothing at all has a level, in a whole
file of "four kinds of nothing". But that fires at zero, and one out of
seventy-two is not zero, so nothing fired and a one-row worklist was served as the
complete answer ([476](issues/476-what-to-reorder-was-watching-one-line-in-seventy-two.md)).
It now carries the denominator — **"71 of your 72 stock lines have no reorder
level"** — and, in the sentence that matters, points her at the screen that DOES
look at everything.

### The same bug again, in a file I had not opened

The dead-stock rule turned up a second time, in `agingReport` rather than
`slowMoverReport`, written the same way and feeding **Stock reports** — a pane
already scored 8 / 9, so somebody had looked at it and this had survived the
look. Found by grepping the module for the shape rather than by clicking, then
driven on her screen to confirm
([477](issues/477-the-reports-screen-aged-stock-that-had-no-age.md)).

Three things on that one screen came off the same root:

- The "priciest items gathering dust" card listed garments that arrived a
  fortnight earlier.
- The window there was a private **90 days** while her Planning settings say
  **180** — two screens describing the same stock by two rules, and the ignored
  one was the number she can actually change.
- **"Money sitting still · 54 lines not sold in over 3 months."** Her real split
  is nought lines in that band and 54 that have never sold. The card sums the two
  buckets for its money, which is fair, then borrowed one band's words for both.

And a fourth found beside them, from a different root: **"How fast it sells
0.0x"**, over 36 units sold in the period. A turn is what the sold goods cost
against the value held, none of what she sold has a cost recorded, so the
numerator was nought and the card said her stock never sells. It already refused
to answer when nothing had sold; it now refuses for this reason too.

Fixing the first of those made a fifth sentence false — the empty state that
replaced the dust card said "everything you hold has sold recently enough",
to a shop where nothing has sold at all. That is the usual cost of a fix and it
was paid in the same pass.

### One that was already right, and was the yardstick

**Cost to keep** needed nothing. It names "68 items have no cost price" in an
amber band, says what that does to its own figures, and prints `No cost set` per
row rather than a confident $0.00. $870.00 at 25% is $217.50, and $17.88 a month
is that over twelve. It is the pane the other three were measured against, and
the reason three of those four defects have an obvious right answer: a neighbour
had already written it.

### One I started to file and should not have

The one row on the reorder list read "Takes 21 days" beside "No supplier yet",
and I began writing it up as a fallback lead time that does not admit itself. The
platform fallback is 14, so 21 had to have come from somewhere — and it had. That
level carries a hand-set lead time of 21 days, a reorder point of 2 and a reorder
quantity of 12, and "To order 12" is that quantity exactly. Every figure on the
row is real. It is the only line in her catalogue somebody has finished setting
up, which is precisely why it is the only one the list can see.

### Where it stands

All six panes seen in light, in dark, and at 360px in an injected iframe:
`scrollWidth === clientWidth === 360` on every one, with the wide tables scrolling
inside their own cards. 360 inventory tests (five new; four of them proven red by
putting the old rule back), api-rest 188, Piggles console 216, sparx console 141. Typecheck clean on the inventory package, api-rest and both consoles.
All ten structural checks pass.

50 of the 56 Stock panes remain unopened. Suppliers, purchase orders and receiving
are the next real job — she has zero of all three, and Partners is an app she has
not switched on.

## Act 120 — Buying it in, and a saved record that kept saying it was not saved

Devi makes her clothes; she does not buy them. So her suppliers are mills and
trim merchants, and she has already told the software about one of them without
knowing it: the cost she recorded in Money on the 9th reads **"Linen and cotton
from Ashcombe Mills, $240.00, Parts & materials"**. Stock had zero suppliers, zero
purchase orders and zero deliveries.

Partners, the app that fronts all of that, is off by default. She never needed to
know: typing "supplier" into the search box returned eight Stock entries with
**Suppliers** first, correctly filed under the app that actually owns them.

### The supplier form scolded her before she typed

It opens with **"A supplier needs a name."** in red under the first field, on a
form she has not touched. Short code, in the same card, waits until there is
something to be wrong about — and four other create forms in the console gate
their errors on a `touched` flag that this one did not have
([479](issues/479-the-form-told-her-off-before-she-typed-anything.md)). The
asterisk stays; the telling-off waits.

### She added the supplier, and the console spent the next minute denying it

Ashcombe Mills saved. The record is in the database, complete. And at the same
moment, on the same screen:

| where             | what it said                  |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| status bar, left  | Saved just now                |
| status bar, right | **Not saved: Ashcombe Mills** |
| the tab           | an unsaved dot                |

Closing the pane asked **"Changes to Ashcombe Mills have not been saved. Close
anyway?"**, and navigating away raised Chrome's own **"Leave site?"** dialog. The
leave-guard is the one thing between an owner and lost work, and this teaches her
it lies ([478](issues/478-she-added-a-supplier-and-was-told-it-was-not-saved.md)).

`target: 'replace'` swaps the pane's params without remounting it, so the load
effect never runs again and the baseline stays empty forever. The mechanism is
written out at length in `staff/person-writes.ts` — _"a saved person carrying an
unsaved dot and a leave-guard on the way out"_ — and in one line above
`crm/object-type-detail`'s own fix. Somebody met this, diagnosed it exactly,
fixed it where they stood, and wrote down why. **Seven panes carry the latch;
four were already correct and three were not.**

The workaround, had she found it, was to press Save a second time.

### A code she mistyped said somebody may have deleted it

"What you buy from this supplier" asks for a product code. She buys linen, so she
typed `linen`. Two messages arrived together:

> No item in your catalog has the code "linen". Check the code and try again.

> **That didn't save** — That no longer exists, someone may have deleted it while
> you had it open.

Nothing was being saved (the lookup is a GET), nothing was deleted, and there is
no someone — she works alone
([480](issues/480-a-code-she-mistyped-said-someone-may-have-deleted-it.md)). The
failed-write net watches every mutation so no failed write is silent, and it only
stays quiet when the call site claims the conversation by passing `shownInPlace`.
This one handled the error in a **try/catch**, which is as invisible to a cache
watcher as a render is. The Recipes pane uses the same lookup and passes its own
handler, so it was already quiet.

### Where the act stops, and why

Two real suppliers now exist — **Ashcombe Mills** (fabric, net 30, 21 days) and
**Fairfield Trims** (the brass hardware for the leather-covered belt, net 15, 10
days). No purchase order has been raised, and that is the honest stopping point
rather than a tidy one.

To raise one she has to say what she buys, and every item she buys is fabric and
findings, none of which are in her catalogue. There is no "not for sale" flag on a
product — a component is presumably a draft product that never reaches the site,
which is what Recipes and Making runs must already assume. **That has not been
driven, so nothing is filed about it.** The inline message she gets is accurate
("check the code"), and whether it should also offer "or add it" depends on
whether a maker can add a raw material without putting it on sale. That is the
next act's first question.

### Where it stands

Three defects found, all three fixed and re-proved on her screen, all mirrored
into the sparx console. Adding Fairfield Trims came back with no unsaved dot, no
"Not saved", Save correctly disabled, and closed without a prompt. Typing `linen`
again produced one message instead of two.

## Act 121 — Buying the fabric, and a $46.80 bill that went in as $4,680

Act 120 stopped on a question: can a maker put a raw material into this software
without putting it on sale? **Yes, and the console says so plainly.** New product
has a switch called "Put it on sale straight away", off by default, under the
sentence _"Leave this off to save it out of sight and finish it first."_ Save it
and the pane opens with a blue band: _"Not on sale — this is saved but hidden,
nobody can see it on your website yet."_ The public site only ever serves active
products, so the words and the code agree. Nothing to file; the answer was
already built.

Getting to that answer, and then buying with it, cost ten defects.

### The form would not let her save and would not say why

She typed a name. The code filled itself in. **Add product stayed grey**, and
nothing anywhere on the form said what was missing
([481](issues/481-add-product-sat-grey-with-nothing-saying-why.md)). The missing
answer was the price, and the sentence saying so — "Give the product a price." —
is written into the file on a branch that can never render. The code beside it
gates its error on "has this form been started", which is the right rule; the
price was held to a different one. None of the three required fields carried the
asterisk that twenty-one other panes use.

Its panel had no name either — the tab read "Product" and the unsaved chip read
**"Not saved: a panel"**, with seven panes open
([482](issues/482-the-new-product-panel-had-no-name-of-its-own.md)). The sparx
twin, which never split this form into its own file, still says "New product".

### The saved-record-that-says-it-is-not-saved defect, in two panes I had cleared

She raised her first purchase order — 40 metres of linen from Ashcombe Mills —
and the toast said **"PO-000001 saved as a draft"** over a tab with an unsaved
dot and a status bar reading **"Not saved: PO-000001"**
([483](issues/483-two-more-panes-saved-a-record-and-kept-denying-it.md)).

That is [478](issues/478-she-added-a-supplier-and-was-told-it-was-not-saved.md),
in a pane 478's own table marked **correct**. So did `finance/expense-detail`,
which is where every cost she records goes. Both files DO carry the rebase. In
both it sits inside the `else`. **Reading a file for the presence of a fix
answers a different question from reading the branch the create path takes**, and
478 recorded the first answer to the second question. Re-measured from the SWAP
rather than the latch: 61 panes swap in place under a dirty guard, 11 hold their
baseline in state, and reading those 11 at the swap found two more broken and
seven right — by three different means, not one. 478's table now says so.

Checking the two orders in the database afterwards turned up the half of that
defect nobody had seen: PO-000001 has **no payment terms** and PO-000002 carries
Fairfield's `net 15`. Creating an order fills the terms from the supplier; the
un-rebased draft kept showing an empty box, and the next save wrote that empty
box back over what the server had worked out. **A stale draft does not only
mis-report its own state, it overwrites everything the server computed.**
PO-000001 now reads net 30, put right through the screen.

### $25.00 of carriage, saved as $201.00

She selected the shipping box, which held `0.00`, and typed `25.00`. It settled
on **`201.00`** and the order total went from $720 to $921
([484](issues/484-a-shipping-charge-typed-as-25-was-saved-as-201.md)). The first
keystroke replaced the selection with `2`, the field reformatted it to `2.00` and
put the caret behind the cents, and every later digit was rounded away. The
field was `MoneyTextInput`, whose whole contract is that the caller owns the
text; this caller owned cents and rebuilt the text on every render, so what she
typed never survived one keystroke. The right component was two fields away, with
a comment naming this exact failure.

### "£4.10 each, or £3.60 if you take fifty"

Four inches under that sentence, on the same card: **"$4.10 each below the first
step"**. Two currencies, one card
([485](issues/485-british-pounds-in-an-american-console.md)). Six places in each
console, including the DEFAULT NAME of a spending limit — `Orders over £1,000` —
which is not a caption but a value, saved into the record and printed to whoever
the held order belongs to.

### She typed 3,60 and the software wrote $360

The ladder's price box was a browser number field. It dropped the comma, took
`360`, saved it, and said _"Purchase orders for Brass belt hardware, antique will
use them from now on."_
([486](issues/486-a-price-of-3-60-was-saved-as-360-dollars.md)) That is issue
086, whose fix is in this repo, whose replacement component exists in both
consoles, and which **thirty-seven money fields had not been migrated to**. They
have now, along with the five near-identical copies of a local `dollarsToCents`
that all read money with `Number()`.

### The ladder she had just set could not reach the order she then raised

The Quantity prices card promises that _"a purchase order picks the right price
for the quantity being ordered — and tells the buyer what the next step down
would save."_ She set $3.60 from fifty, then ordered sixty, and the line came out
at **$4.10 each, $246.00**
([487](issues/487-the-quantity-price-ladder-never-reached-an-order.md)).

The server resolves ladders correctly, with a tested function, under one stated
condition: _"Only consulted when the buyer did not type a cost — an explicit
figure is a negotiated one and always wins."_ That is a good rule, and the screen
defeated it by filling the required cost box with the base price the moment an
item was picked. **The screen was typing a price on her behalf and the server was
treating it as hers.** The dialog now prices the line from the ladder at the
quantity, using the server's own function, until she types a figure of her own —
and says which rung it used, or what the next one would save.

### And then her books

She recorded thread, interfacing and buttons: `46,80`. "Cost recorded." The row
says **468000** — four thousand six hundred and eighty dollars, in a month whose
whole spending was $2,090
([488](issues/488-a-46-dollar-cost-went-into-the-books-as-4680.md)).

The money parser threw every comma away before looking at the number. `1,250` is
twelve fifty, which is right; `46,80` is four thousand six hundred and eighty,
which is not. And the OTHER money parser, forty lines away in `read-money.ts`,
knows exactly which of `.` and `,` separates the cents — it has a documented
function whose only job is that question — and then finishes with
`Math.round(Number(x) * 100)`, which reads $0.145 as 14¢. **Each parser had the
half the other was missing, and a docblock explaining why its half mattered.**
There is one parser now, with both halves, and sixteen tests; two of them go red
if either half is removed.

The cost form also greeted her with **"Say what the money was spent on."** in red
on an untouched field ([489](issues/489-the-cost-form-told-her-off-before-she-typed.md)),
and offered **"Brake pads for the Henderson job"** as the example of what a cost
looks like, to a woman who sews
([490](issues/490-the-examples-on-two-forms-were-somebody-elses-trade.md)).

### Where it stands

Two purchase orders exist and stay: **PO-000001**, 40 linen at $18.00 with $25.00
carriage, $745.00 to Ashcombe Mills on net 30; **PO-000002**, 60 brass buckles at
the ladder price of $3.60, $216.00 to Fairfield Trims on net 15. Two raw
materials are in the catalogue and off the website. One cost is recorded, and it
is recorded correctly.

Neither order has been PLACED. Placing one is the next act's first move, and
receiving what arrives against it is the move after that — which is the first
time any of her stock numbers will have come from something she bought rather
than something she counted.

## Interlude — two defects in the workspace itself, reported by Brandon

Not Devi's, and not found by driving her console: found by WATCHING one being
driven. Both are in the chassis every pane sits in, so they were on screen for
every act of this journal and never once written down.

The scrollbars around the workspace flickered and then stayed on. The canvas was
being given a pixel size equal to the frame's own visible width, and
`clientWidth` is a rounded integer — so the value written back was a fraction
wider than the box it came from, which conjured a scrollbar, which shrank the
box, which conjured the other one
([491](issues/491-the-workspace-scrollbars-flickered-over-content-that-fits.md)).

Then, with nineteen panes open, switching from windows back to tabs tiled the
screen into nineteen 90px columns whose tab strips had no room for a word. A
window coming back was asking dockview for a NEW group each time, and windows
mode gives every pane a window of its own, so N panes meant N columns. Worse, it
kept coming back after a reload, because by then the nineteen slivers had been
photographed as the saved tab arrangement
([492](issues/492-switching-windows-back-to-tabs-gave-every-pane-a-sliver.md)).

**Merging them fixed the slivers and broke the next thing in the same breath.**
Moving a group into another leaves the host with no ACTIVE panel: nineteen tabs
across the top, every one inactive, and dockview's "nothing open" watermark
under them — a full tab strip over a blank screen. That is recorded in 492
rather than quietly repaired, because "a group with no active panel" is not a
state anybody can reach by clicking, and the next person to move a group needs
to know it is a state code can reach.

Both comments involved were RIGHT about the call in front of them and silent
about what happens when it runs nineteen times. That is the same shape as
[478](issues/478-she-added-a-supplier-and-was-told-it-was-not-saved.md) clearing
two panes whose fix sits in the `else`.

## Act 122 — Seventy-three lines of stock, and sixty-nine warnings she had not earned

Purchasing is closed until the freight migration is run, so she went to look at
what she already has. The linen was there: **38 metres, at Main Warehouse.**

Everything around it was on fire.

Of seventy-three lines, **sixty-nine wore a colored badge and fifty-six of those
were red** — a number of hours or days, in amber or red, next to a quantity, with
no tooltip, no legend and no header explaining what was being counted.

The component's own comment said the badge showed "how long since anybody
checked". It did not. It measured how long since the quantity last MOVED, and a
sale moves it. Nobody looks at a shelf when an order is placed.

Which makes the whole thing run backwards. Asking her ledger which lines had
genuinely been counted:

```
THE-ASH-OVER-M-SLATE   green, no badge     really counted 16 days ago
THE-ASH-OVER-M-CLAY    green, no badge     really counted 16 days ago
MARLOW-KNIT-L-OAT      green, no badge     really counted 16 days ago
```

**The three lines with no warning at all were the ones nobody had checked in over
a fortnight.** They sold that day, so they looked fresh. The loud ones were the
stock that simply was not selling — the stock least likely to have drifted,
because nobody had touched it. What makes a book number drift from a shelf is
handling, and handling is what selling is.

And the deadline was invented. Under a day fine, under a week amber, over a week
red. Devi had **no counting schedule at all**. She was being marked against a
promise she never made — which the same file already knows is wrong, one function
above, where a data feed with no declared interval gets no verdict at all rather
than a reassuring tick ([498](issues/498-a-sale-is-not-a-stock-check.md)).

So a verdict now needs a promise, the ledger's real `recount` is now carried
through to the screen, and the pane says the thing none of the numbers could:
**"Last counted against the shelf 2 weeks ago."**

Then, because a guard that cannot go red is not proven, she set up a real
routine — and walked straight into the next one.

**Set one up** handed her a form already filled in: _Fulfillment Center_, _Top-value
stock only_. Fulfillment Center holds **nothing**; all seventy-three lines are at
Main Warehouse. And her stock is **all class C**, because ABC is worked out from a
year of usage she has not had yet, so "top value" is empty by construction.

The pre-filled setup covered zero items on two separate counts, and Set it up
would have saved it without a word. The counts would simply never have arrived —
the exact failure the feature exists to prevent, since a schedule is what turns
counting from an intention into a fact.

The number that catches it already existed. The SAVED schedule's pane says
"73 items currently covered". It was being shown after the decision instead of
during it. Now the form asks the same question as she types, and says either
"73 items would be covered by this" or refuses to stay quiet:

> **Nothing is covered by this**
> There is no stock at this location in this group, so this schedule would never
> raise a count.

([499](issues/499-a-counting-schedule-that-covers-nothing.md))

She set up _Everything at Main, weekly_, and the stock list came back honest: her
linen marked **Never counted** (received, never checked), the four Ash Overshirts
counted yesterday marked nothing at all, and the fortnight-old lines marked
**Count due 10 days ago**. Exactly inverted from where it started.

One of the two defects on that screen was mine. The first run printed **"Count due
NaN days ago"** on every row, because `intervalDays === null` is not the test when
the value crosses a network that can simply omit the field. It was caught in the
only way it could be: by looking at the screen.

## Act 123 — Sixty brass buckles, and a red band she should have read sooner

The buckles from Fairfield Trims had been sitting unreceived for days. Fifty-eight
turned up good and two came through with the antique plating scratched down to
the brass, so she booked them in that way and added the courier's $14.00 as a
cost on the delivery.

Everything the console promised her came true, which is worth saying plainly
because it usually is not the story here:

```
PO-000002   partly received   58 of 60, 2 still to come
movements   receive +58 · receive +2 · damage -2
on hand     58 at $3.84 each
```

The damaged pair are recorded as having arrived and then written off, exactly as
the note beside the field said they would be, and the order stayed open because
Fairfield still owes her two. The delivery said **$208.80 for the goods, $14.00
getting them here, $222.80 what this stock is worth** — and the empty state that
[500](issues/500-the-receipt-denied-the-freight-it-was-showing.md) fixed read
correctly on the previous delivery, which is the last thing that had been left
unseen from the freight work.

Except the row itself could not be added up.

> Brass belt hardware · 58 units · **$3.60** invoiced · plus **$14.00** · really
> cost **$3.84** each

Invoiced is per unit. Really cost is per unit. The middle column was the line's
whole share. The same row on the linen read $18.00 · $1.25 · $18.63 and nobody
noticed, because **$1.25 is small enough to look like a per-unit number**. $14.00
against $3.60 is not, so the second delivery showed what the first had hidden
([502](issues/502-three-numbers-on-a-row-that-could-not-be-added.md)). It now
reads $0.24, with "$14.00 in all" underneath, and 3.60 + 0.24 = 3.84.

### The band she had been scrolling past

Across the top of every screen, in red, all session:

> **Your site is offline. It comes back as soon as a payment goes through.**

It is true. Her trial ended on 6 September and the grace window closed on the
13th. A `curl` said her site returned **200**, which for a few minutes looked like
the console crying wolf — and proved nothing at all, because the "back soon"
overlay IS a 200 page. Opening it in a browser settled it in ten seconds.

What the overlay does not do is tell anybody else. Asked what a crawler gets:

```
<title>       Juniper Row, small-batch clothing made in Denver
description   Shirts, dresses and knitwear cut and sewn by hand in a Denver studio...
robots        index, follow
robots.txt    every crawler welcome, eleven AI crawlers by name, sitemap advertised
sitemap.xml   43 URLs
```

Forty-three real pages, offered to the whole internet under her own name, every
one of them now blank. That is worse than being offline. Being offline is
temporary; being re-indexed is not. She pays the bill, the shop comes back, and
the listings are gone.

The layout DOES set `noindex` for a dark site, with a comment explaining why. It
cannot win: a route's metadata overrides a layout's, and five page routes write
`index: true` outright. **A base a page can overwrite is not a guard**
([503](issues/503-a-dark-site-still-invited-the-crawlers.md)). Eight page routes
and all three crawler routes now answer as a dark site before they say anything
about her.

### And what her customers were reading

> **Catching a fresh spark**
> This site is taking a short break and will be back shortly.

The spark is the sparx mark. The file's own comment, twelve lines above, explains
that there must be no sparx logo because a platform-branded takeover of a
tenant's dark site advertises exactly what the overlay exists to hide. The logo
was removed and the same advertisement left behind in words — on a Denver
clothing label reached through Piggles, which is not even the right platform.

It also said nothing. A shopper who wanted a shirt learns nothing from a pun
about a company she has never heard of. And the only sentence on the page was set
in a grey the house rules reserve for text not meant to be read.

It now says **"Back soon"**
([504](issues/504-the-dark-page-carried-a-platform-pun.md)). `docs/17` specified
the sparx-flavored line and has been corrected to say why it must not be.

### One from last session that had been written down instead of fixed

The covered-items count [499](issues/499-a-counting-schedule-that-covers-nothing.md)
added counts by location and class. The form also offers "narrow to one zone",
and the generator honours it. The count did not. Devi has three zones and every
one of them is empty, so all three read **73 items covered** over a schedule that
would raise nothing — the number built to catch an empty schedule being the thing
that hid one ([501](issues/501-the-coverage-count-could-not-see-a-zone.md)).

It had been recorded last session as "over-reports" and left. Recording is not
the work, and "over-reports" was too gentle for a figure that is wrong by the
whole of itself.

## Act 124 — The warning she needed was cut off, and so was the rest of the form

Proving the zone fix meant typing a zone into the schedule and watching the count
fall to nothing. It did. The warning appeared, and it was **cut off mid-sentence**
by the bottom of its own card.

Asked what else that pane was hiding, in a 908px window:

```
card                              shown   real    hidden
What to call it / Which location    142     220      78
What it covers                      252     410     158
How often, and how much at a time   288     471     183
History                              88     128      40
                                                  -----
                                                    459
```

**Four hundred and fifty-nine pixels of her form, unreachable.** The location
dropdown among them: the label on screen, the control under it gone. And the pane
reported that it fitted, so there was no scrollbar to find any of it with.

`PANE_SHELL` is a flex column, silica's `.card` sets `overflow: hidden`, and per
the flexbox spec that makes `min-height: auto` resolve to 0. The guard that stops
a flex item shrinking below its content is switched off by the very property that
then hides what overflows. So the column squeezed every card flat instead of
scrolling — and got worse as content grew, which is backwards: the warning that
only appears when something is wrong is what pushed it over the edge.

The answer was one file away. `pane-toolbar.tsx` already carries `[&>*]:shrink-0`
on the toolbar row for exactly this reason. It had never been carried to the shell
around it ([505](issues/505-a-pane-that-scrolled-squeezed-its-cards-flat.md)).
There is now a named `PANE_SHELL_SCROLL`, and the seven panes per console that
were hand-rolling the scrolling shell use it. After: 1297px of content in a 908px
pane, a scrollbar, and every card hiding nothing.

### And once she could read the warning, it told her to fix the wrong thing

> There is no stock at this location **in this group**. Try **"Everything at this
> location"**, or **pick the place your stock actually sits**.

Her group was already "Everything at this location" and her location was the only
one with stock in it. The **zone** was the problem, and the zone is not mentioned.
Both remedies leave the zone box untouched, so doing as it says changes nothing
and the warning stays up — which teaches her the console is broken rather than
that her setup is
([506](issues/506-the-warning-named-the-wrong-control.md)). It now names whichever
of the three controls is actually narrowing it, and how to widen that one. All
four combinations proven on screen.

The first version of that fix printed "…would never raise a count. **choose**
'Everything at this location'" — lowercase, because the remedies were phrased to
follow "Clear the zone box, or …" and nothing capitalised whichever one led. My
own, caught by reading the sentence after changing one dropdown. That is twice in
one session that the only thing standing between a fix and a fresh defect was
looking at it.

### One left open on purpose

Putting the form back exactly as she found it left the status bar still saying
**"Not saved"**, and closing would still have asked her to confirm discarding
changes she had already undone. The flag is a sticky boolean: it means "somebody
touched something", never "this differs from what is stored".

That is the house pattern across about **120 panes**, not a slip in one, and the
risk is lopsided — the bug costs one unnecessary dialog, and a botched replacement
costs somebody's work. Filed with the measurement rather than patched in one pane
and left inconsistent in a hundred and nineteen
([507](issues/507-undo-your-edits-and-it-still-says-unsaved.md)).

## Act 125 — Looking for the delivery she had just booked

She wanted GR-000003 back, so she typed its number into the box at the top of the
console. The one headed **Search everything**.

> Nothing matches that. Try a different word.
> Nothing in your **orders**, customers or products matches "GR-000003".

Then PO-000002. Then "Fairfield". Then LINEN-NAT-200, a code off her own stock
list. Nothing, every time.

The universal index carries twenty kinds of record, plus customers and sales
orders. **None of them is from purchasing.** No orders to suppliers, no
deliveries, no suppliers, no stock levels, no counts, no transfers, no bills. The
whole module she has spent four acts working in is invisible to the only search
box in the product.

And the sentence made it worse. "Nothing in your **orders** matches PO-000002" is
read by an owner as _your orders do not contain it_. Hers do. It was never
searched: "orders" there means orders from CUSTOMERS, and she had typed an order
to a SUPPLIER, with no way to tell the two readings apart. The honest conclusion
available to her was that the record had gone
([508](issues/508-search-everything-cannot-find-a-purchase-order.md)).

It now says what it looked through and names what it did not, so she goes to Stock
instead of searching again. **And the sparx console turned out to be a step
further back**: it runs the same record search and had no note at all, so its
record half said nothing whatever. That is the defect the Piggles version was
written to fix, still shipping next door. Ported and proven there too, in sparx's
own words. Making purchasing searchable is a separate call: it
adds documents to the index for every tenant, which is ongoing cost.

(The index is also empty locally, 4 documents across 113 tenants, because
`sparx-nats` is unhealthy and indexing is event-driven. That is this machine, not
the product. The scope finding is from the projector registry, not the empty
index.)

## Act 126 — The console accused Fairfield Trims of overcharging her

Entering a supplier's invoice is meant to be one field: the number off the paper.
Everything else is filled in. So she filled in the number.

> **They are asking for $222.72**
> The check: **1 line(s) do not agree** · **$13.92 more than the goods justify**
>
> Brass belt hardware · ordered 60 · arrived 58 · billed 58 · **$3.84, agreed
> $3.60** · **Charged more than agreed $13.92**
>
> Either accept the difference, which is recorded against your name, or query it
> with the supplier, which stops it being paid.

Fairfield billed the agreed $3.60. **The $13.92 is her own courier bill**, which
the console put inside the supplier's invoice and then flagged as the supplier's
overcharge. The draft seeded each line with the LANDED cost, and the match
compares a bill line against the ORDER's agreed price, so the variance is exactly
the freight, on every order that carries any
([509](issues/509-the-console-accused-her-supplier-of-overcharging.md)). The same
panel has its own Freight box underneath, so filling that in as intended would
have counted the carriage twice.

Her two doors were both wrong: sign her name to an overcharge that never happened,
or email a supplier to dispute a correct invoice and stop paying it.

### And she could not simply fix the number

The panel says, in its own words, "Correct anything the paper says differently".
The table was read-only text. Not editable there, and not afterwards either,
where the only actions are accept, query, or cancel the lot.

Its docblock had already written down why that matters:

> The panel fills in OUR side and asks the operator to correct it to THEIRS. ...
> A bill created straight from the receipt would match the receipt perfectly by
> construction, **and a match that cannot fail is not a check.**

And the endpoint has always taken a `lines` array, its schema commented "what the
operator corrected the draft to". Nothing ever sent one. So the three-way match
compared our numbers against our numbers, and the check that cannot fail was the
one that shipped.

Both halves are fixed. The draft carries the supplier's price, the lines are
editable, and the column reads **Billed** rather than Received. Proven on the
linen: pre-filled $18.00 / $36.00 where it would have said $18.63 / $37.25, and
agreeing with the "$36.00 what the goods cost" four inches above it. Typing 18.50
moved the total to $37.00 and back again.

One thing it does not fix. That invoice covers 2 metres of an order for 40, so
the check now flags the QUANTITY instead: "Billed for less than arrived · $684.00
in your favour", on a perfectly correct partial invoice
([510](issues/510-a-partial-invoice-reads-as-a-disagreement.md)). What the match
should compare on a multi-delivery order is a decision, not a patch, and the
failure mode of getting it wrong is missing a supplier who really does short-ship
and bill in full.

A reopened pane lands at the END of the strip rather than where it was closed from; noted, not filed, because reopening and re-placing are different promises and only the first is made.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Dates                        | **Done — both halves driven, and the second half was broken.** Machine is UTC−7 (PDT). Devi's console shows SPRING15's stored `2026-10-01 06:59 UTC` as **09/30/2026 11:59 PM**, correct in her own time. **The last hour works**: sale ending 00:04, code applied at 23:21:38 for −$20.70. **The first hour after did not refuse it.** At 23:22, an hour past the end, the basket still showed the code, every checkout step showed the saving, and the button placed **O-000011 at $126.30 against a sale that ended at 22:21** — while Devi's own Discounts list correctly read **Ended**. [300], major: the window was checked only when the code was TYPED. Proving it turned up [301] as well — a code typed after checkout began never reached the total, because the session froze the money at `start()` and nothing refreshed it. Both fixed together: the basket sheds a lapsed saving on read and on every mutation, an in-flight session is kept in line with its basket, the order is priced from the settled basket, and the button's own total is sent back so nothing can be written for a figure she was never shown. Re-run: the same press now answers _"The total changed while you were checking out. Open your basket to see what it comes to now."_ and writes nothing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Money edge                   | **Done, and it produced the run's worst defect.** Built the named case — a discounted order on the free-shipping threshold — as Anneliese: $110 trouser + $42 tee = $152.00, over her $150 line so shipping was free, then SPRING15 for −$22.80. Cart, all three checkout steps and the button itself said **$129.20**. The order written said **$152.00, discount 0.00**, and so did her order history and Devi's console, which showed no discount line at all and no sign a code had been used. The code was still spent: a $22.80 redemption row, usage count 2, `per_customer_limit` 1. [298], blocker. `computeTotals` had no discount parameter while `CreateOrderInput` declared one — accepted, validated, never read, with `taxTotal` beside it carrying exactly the override discount was missing. Two callers believed in it, checkout and the orders CSV import. Fixed at the spine plus a per-line apportionment so a refund has the right basis, and re-proved as Jo at $138.00: button $126.30, order 138.00 / −20.70 / +9.00 / **126.30**, lines $14.40 and $6.30 off. **On the threshold question itself: free shipping reads the PRE-discount subtotal.** Anneliese shipped free while paying $129.20; Jo's $138.00 was charged $9.00. Consistent, and both readings of "free over $150" are defensible, so recorded rather than filed — Devi has never been asked which she means.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Buyer's side                 | **Done, and it was the richest hour of the run — six defects.** Anneliese had no login, so she made one; the signup matched her existing customer row rather than duplicating it, and her order was there. Everything around it was wrong: the shop said **Sign in** to her on every page and gave her no route to her account ([291]); her order showed the full $170 and "Payment Partially Paid" without ever mentioning the $42 refunded ([292]); the status card drew three black rules across itself ([293]); the order list rendered as a centered stack ([294]); one screen called the same event `fulfilled`, `Fulfilled` and `Shipped` ([295]). Fixing [291] then exposed [296] — the whole upgrade-on-read that heals stale chrome had never been called by anything. **Self-service returns did not exist** on the storefront -- the only path was Requests -> "Ask for help", which is the three messages back and forth Devi came here to stop. Brandon called it into scope, and it is now built and seeded ([297]): a customer picks lines, a reason and refund-or-swap from the order itself, both sides can follow it, and the shop is told. That closes her third goal.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Someone else's business      | **Done, and nothing leaked.** Searched `Thistle`, `sourdough` and `Lindqvist` -- "Nothing in your orders, customers or products matches" each time. Deep-linked Thistle & Rye's product and order ids: both refused, 404, RLS re-checked as the app role (0 rows). The site switcher offers only Juniper Row. Two defects in what the refusal SAID -- [286], [287].
